book.title: The Penguin Book of Financial Times Crosswords, volume 1

parts.note: par is the average or normal standard
the suffix -ish means fairly or somewhat

explanation.surface: Someone describes an unremarkable, middling sort of neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fairly average' reads as par-ish: about par. 'Kind of' just joins wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A parish is a local administrative or church area, a small district of a county or diocese.

clue.text: Bit of a mixed-up type goes to church

parts.note: printers' pie is jumbled type
CE, the Church of England

explanation.surface: A confused person starts attending church.
explanation.walkthrough: Pie, also spelt pi, is a printer's term for a heap of type all mixed up.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece is a portion or fragment of something, a bit of it.

clue.text: Building which could daunt or confuse

indicators.note: to confuse is to muddle, so the preceding letters get jumbled into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A building so imposing it might intimidate or bewilder visitors.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotunda is a round building, usually domed, so it is a kind of building.

definitions.meaning: surface reading: a very appropriate area of the capital
setter's reading: a London street full of suits, home of the tailors

explanation.walkthrough: Savile Row is the Mayfair street famous for bespoke tailoring; 'suitable' is read as full of suits.
explanation.definitionFit: The street is where London's finest made-to-measure gentlemen's suits are cut and sewn.

parts.note: AC, short for account, which is a bill
a price is what something costs

explanation.surface: Someone is told to go and say hello to a man called Bill Price.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill Price looks like a person's name; it is two separate words, account and cost.
explanation.definitionFit: To accost is to approach someone and speak to them, often boldly or uninvited.

definitions.meaning: the line with its gap, where a word for a set of beliefs belongs
the source: the sonnet The World Is Too Much With Us

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap from the poem: Wordsworth would rather be a pagan raised in an outdated faith.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is a set of religious beliefs, which fits suckled in and outworn.

parts.note: the outward leg of the journey
the return leg: a two-way ticket is out and back

explanation.surface: A return ticket to the Australian wilderness.
explanation.walkthrough: A two-way ticket takes you out and brings you back.
explanation.definitionFit: The outback is the remote, sparsely settled interior of Australia, its wild bush country.

clue.text: Twice set about winger with lethal attack

definitions.text: Twice set about winger with lethal attack

indicators.note: twice asks for the rearranged word to be written two times
about means around in a new order, so set is rearranged

parts.note: a fly is a winged insect, a winger

explanation.surface: Something with wings deals a deadly bite, twice set upon its victims.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges SET into TSE; 'Twice' doubles it, then FLY.
explanation.definitionFit: This African insect spreads sleeping sickness through its bite, a winged creature with deadly attack.

clue.text: Uneasy at support I have obtained

parts.note: a rest is a support, as for a cue or an arm
the contraction I've

explanation.surface: Someone feels uncomfortable about the backing they have managed to secure.
explanation.definitionFit: Restive describes someone restless, fidgety and unable to settle, which is being uneasy.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: irritated, put out
second meaning: stung by the stinging plant

explanation.surface: Someone is cross about having been stung.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is literal: brushed against stinging nettles.
explanation.definitionFit: Nettled means irritated in everyday speech, and literally describes skin stung by the weed.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a man bearing a visible mark
second meaning: someone targeted, as by an opponent or assassin

explanation.surface: The gangster Scarface is picked out by the authorities.
explanation.definitionFit: A marked man is one with a physical mark, or one targeted for revenge or close watching.

clue.text: She's in the dog-house at work

definitions.meaning: surface reading: a woman is in disgrace with someone
setter's reading: her job literally keeps her among the dogs in their kennels

explanation.walkthrough: To be 'in the dog-house' usually means being out of favour; here it is a woman's literal workplace.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman employed to look after dogs at boarding kennels works in a house for dogs.

clue.text: Torn from cheap service guide found in church

indicators.note: something torn from a longer run of words is ripped out of the middle of it

parts.note: lies across the end of cheap and the start of service

explanation.surface: A page is ripped out of a cheap order-of-service booklet found in a church.
explanation.definitionFit: The apse is the vaulted semicircular recess at the east end of a church, so it is found there.

parts.note: CH is the standard abbreviation for church
an air is a tune

explanation.surface: Someone runs a meeting about church music.
explanation.definitionFit: To chair a meeting is to preside over it, running and conducting its business.

clue.text: Don't shout so much when miserable

parts.note: a shout of encouragement or applause
do it less

explanation.surface: Advice to keep the noise down when someone is unhappy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don't shout so much' is read as an instruction: cheer less.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheerless means gloomy and joyless, lacking any comfort, so miserable.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: stop working for the day
second meaning: steal

explanation.surface: Someone will stop work only if really pressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At a pinch' looks like the idiom for 'if necessary'; pinch is really slang for steal.
explanation.definitionFit: To knock off is informal both for ending the working day and for stealing something.

clue.text: Edge away from one's regular job

definitions.meaning: first meaning: at the margin or border, as a position
second meaning: as a sideline, done in addition to a main occupation

explanation.surface: Someone sidles out of the office, slipping away from their usual work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edge away' reads as one verb phrase, but Edge stands alone as the first definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something placed on the side sits at the margin, and money earned on the side comes from extra work.

clue.text: Given finest ring before getting married

parts.note: finest means best
the letter O is ring-shaped
wed means married

explanation.surface: A bride receives her best ring just before the wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: Bestowed means conferred or presented as a gift, the same as given.

parts.note: Ted is short for Edward
IOUs are written acknowledgments of debt

explanation.surface: A dull man named Edward who owes money.
explanation.definitionFit: Tedious means tiresome and monotonous, the same as boring.

parts.note: a test is a trial
the suffix -y makes an adjective meaning being so, having that quality

explanation.surface: A court case has made someone irritable.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as 'test-y', like a trial.
explanation.definitionFit: Testy describes someone irritable and short-tempered, quick to snap.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the backdrop or environment
second meaning: placing something down

explanation.surface: A pleasant spot suited to golf on the green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting' suggests golf; here it is putting as in placing.
explanation.definitionFit: A setting is the surroundings of something, and setting a thing down means putting it.

clue.text: Notice put out by railways on the nail

parts.note: BR, British Rail, formerly British Railways
an ad is a notice published, put out after the railway letters

explanation.surface: A railway notice has been pinned up on a nail.
explanation.walkthrough: A brad is a thin flat-headed nail, a word mostly seen in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A brad is a small slender wire nail with a small head, used in carpentry.

clue.text: Memorial to wine by the sound of it

parts.note: Graves is a Bordeaux wine region and its wine
a tone is a sound

explanation.surface: A monument raised to a wine, judging by how it sounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By the sound of it' suggests a homophone, but here tone is simply a sound placed after the wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A gravestone is the inscribed stone over a grave, a memorial to the dead person.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ... Darling, the lighthouse keeper's daughter who rescued shipwrecked sailors
second meaning: Your ..., the form of address for a duke

explanation.surface: A sweet girl delivers a fine speech.
explanation.walkthrough: Darling is a surname here: Grace Darling was a Victorian heroine of a sea rescue off Northumberland.
explanation.definitionFit: Grace is the girl's first name, and Your Grace is how a duke or archbishop is addressed.

indicators.note: troubled means disturbed, so the letters that follow are stirred into another order

parts.note: Spanish for a gentleman, letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A worried Spanish gentleman struggles with a foreign language.
explanation.definitionFit: Norse, the old Scandinavian language, is a tongue few people know today.

clue.text: Gentlemanly place in Italy requires a pound for drug

parts.note: Shakespeare's Two Gentlemen of Verona
L, libra, the symbol for pound

explanation.surface: A refined Italian town demands payment of a pound for medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: Veronal is the old trade name for barbitone, a sleeping drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Veronal was a barbiturate sold as a sedative and sleeping pill early last century, so a drug.

clue.text: See frozen heroine weep when taking off

parts.note: the heroine of La Bohème, whose tiny hand is frozen
to weep is to cry

explanation.surface: An opera heroine left out in the cold sheds tears as a plane departs.
explanation.walkthrough: In Puccini's La Bohème Rodolfo sings 'Che gelida manina', your tiny hand is frozen, to Mimi.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking off a person means imitating them for comic effect, which is mimicry.

parts.note: SY is the old postal abbreviation for the county of Surrey
a stem is a branch or stalk

explanation.surface: A procedure adopted by the Surrey office of a firm.
explanation.walkthrough: Surrey is a county just south of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A system is an organised method or scheme for doing something.

clue.text: Concert in which Leeds and Sheffield are united

definitions.meaning: first meaning: alliance, as in acting in concert

definitions.text: in which Leeds and Sheffield are united
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the football competition containing clubs called United

explanation.walkthrough: Leeds United and Sheffield United are English football clubs, and both play in the same football competition.
explanation.definitionFit: A league is an alliance of parties acting together, and also a football division grouping clubs.
